theme: Guard the deposit; rightly handling the word
readingInstruction: Read 2 Timothy 1:1-2:26. This is Paul’s last letter, written from prison with death near. Notice the tenderness toward Timothy, the call to guard the gospel, and the pictures of the faithful servant: soldier, athlete, farmer, worker.
settingTheScene: Second Timothy was written around AD 66 to 67, during Paul’s second imprisonment in Rome, probably shortly before his execution. Unlike his first imprisonment, this one is harsh, and Paul is alone except for Luke. He writes to Timothy, his beloved child in the faith, to strengthen him to carry on, to guard the gospel, and to be willing to suffer. It is a farewell letter and a passing of the torch.
observation: “For God gave us a spirit not of fear but of power and love and self-control” (1:7).
“Who saved us and called us to a holy calling, not because of our works but because of his own purpose and grace” (1:9).
“For I know whom I have believed, and I am convinced that he is able to guard until that day what has been entrusted to me” (1:12).
“By the Holy Spirit who dwells within us, guard the good deposit entrusted to you” (1:14).
“And what you have heard from me in the presence of many witnesses entrust to faithful men, who will be able to teach others also” (2:2).
“Share in suffering as a good soldier of Christ Jesus” (2:3).
“Do your best to present yourself to God as one approved, a worker who has no need to be ashamed, rightly handling the word of truth” (2:15).
“The Lord’s servant must not be quarrelsome but kind to everyone, able to teach, patiently enduring evil” (2:24).
interpretation:
Paul begins with thanks and longing. He remembers Timothy’s tears, recalls the sincere faith that lived in his grandmother Lois and mother Eunice, and reminds him to fan into flame the gift of God that is in him. “For God gave us a spirit not of fear but of power and love and self-control.” Timothy seems to have been timid. Fear is not from God, and the Spirit gives courage, love, and discipline. “Therefore do not be ashamed of the testimony about our Lord, nor of me his prisoner, but share in suffering for the gospel by the power of God.”

Then a summary of the gospel: God “saved us and called us to a holy calling, not because of our works but because of his own purpose and grace, which he gave us in Christ Jesus before the ages began, and which now has been manifested through the appearing of our Savior Christ Jesus, who abolished death and brought life and immortality to light through the gospel.” Paul is not ashamed, even in a dungeon: “For I know whom I have believed, and I am convinced that he is able to guard until that day what has been entrusted to me.” Faith is knowing a person. Paul urges Timothy to follow the pattern of sound words and to guard the good deposit by the Holy Spirit. Some, like Phygelus and Hermogenes, have turned away. Onesiphorus, however, was not ashamed of Paul’s chains and refreshed him often, and Paul prays mercy on his household.

Chapter 2 builds on the picture of ministry as hard work. Timothy is to be strengthened by the grace in Christ Jesus and to pass on the gospel: “What you have heard from me in the presence of many witnesses entrust to faithful men, who will be able to teach others also.” Four generations appear here: Paul, Timothy, faithful men, and others. Discipleship is multiplication. Then three images: the soldier, who avoids civilian entanglements to please his commander; the athlete, who competes by the rules; the farmer, who works hard before sharing the crops. Each requires single-mindedness, discipline, and patience. “Remember Jesus Christ, risen from the dead, the offspring of David, as preached in my gospel, for which I am suffering, bound with chains. But the word of God is not bound!”

Paul quotes a trustworthy saying: “If we have died with him, we will also live with him; if we endure, we will also reign with him; if we deny him, he also will deny us; if we are faithless, he remains faithful, for he cannot deny himself.” Timothy is to avoid quarrels about words and irreverent babble. “Do your best to present yourself to God as one approved, a worker who has no need to be ashamed, rightly handling the word of truth.” Some have swerved from the truth, like Hymenaeus and Philetus, who say the resurrection has already happened. But “God’s firm foundation stands, bearing this seal: The Lord knows those who are his.” The household of God contains vessels for honor and for dishonor; Timothy is to cleanse himself, flee youthful passions, and pursue righteousness, faith, love, and peace. The Lord’s servant must be kind, patient, and gentle in correcting opponents, in the hope that God may grant them repentance.
connection: Acts 16:1-3 introduces Timothy and his mother. 1 Timothy 1:18 and 4:14 refer to his gift. Romans 1:16 says Paul is not ashamed of the gospel. Titus 3:5-7 echoes salvation by mercy and not works. Ephesians 1:4 speaks of grace given before the ages. 1 Corinthians 9:24-27 uses the athlete image. Philippians 2:25 and Philemon 2 use soldier language. Numbers 16:5 is quoted in 2:19. Matthew 28:19-20 gives the mission of making disciples. Romans 6:8 and 8:17 parallel the faithful saying.
application:
Name a fear that holds you back and ask God for his spirit of power, love, and self-control.

Think of the people who passed the faith to you. Write to one to thank them. Then think of who you might pass it to.

Which picture fits you today: soldier, athlete, farmer, or worker? Take one step in that direction.
prayerPrompts: Thank God for giving you a spirit of power, love, and self-control.
Ask him to help you guard the good deposit.
Ask him to help you handle his word rightly.
